Left ptosis after 2 minutes ice pack

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: right palpebral fissure improved 3 mm and left improved 2 mm after 2 minutes of ice application. A positive ice pack test is consistent with ptosis due to impaired neuromuscular junction transmission

findings.description: MRI mediastinum: T1, T2 fat-saturated, in-phase and opposed-phase chemical-shift sequences; no gadolinium.

Bilobed thymic tissue 3.2 x 1.8 cm, homogeneous, isointense to muscle on T1, mildly hyperintense on T2, with uniform signal loss on opposed-phase images. Chemical shift ratio 0.61; signal intensity index 34%. No nodular component, cyst or capsule.

output.impression: Homogeneous thymic tissue with uniform signal loss on opposed-phase imaging (chemical shift ratio 0.61), consistent with thymic hyperplasia. No feature of thymoma.

above about 80 cmH2O for age and sex

output.impression: Normal vital capacity (59.6 mL/kg) and normal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures.
recommended_actions: Repeat if bulbar or respiratory symptoms progress.

alternatives: If rate control is still needed and MG worsens, a cardioselective beta-blocker at low dose with monitoring; beta-blockade can usually be withdrawn once euthyroid.
interactions: Pyridostigmine with propranolol: additive bradycardia and AV-nodal slowing; monitor heart rate and rhythm when pyridostigmine is started or increased.

Propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) in myasthenia gravis: beta-blockers, oral or ophthalmic, have been reported to worsen neuromuscular transmission; use with caution at the lowest effective dose and monitor for worsening.
Pyridostigmine with methimazole: no known interaction. Methimazole has no effect on neuromuscular transmission.
Pyridostigmine with selenium or artificial tears: no known interaction.
warnings: High-dose corticosteroids, including IV methylprednisolone pulses, can transiently worsen myasthenia gravis in the first 1 to 2 weeks; pyridostigmine does not prevent this. Start high-dose steroids only with inpatient monitoring of bulbar and respiratory function.
Methimazole: agranulocytosis is a rare serious adverse effect; fever or sore throat needs an urgent white cell count.
Iodinated contrast media can aggravate hyperthyroidism and, rarely, myasthenia gravis.
Myasthenia gravis: avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium where possible; neuromuscular blockers need reduced doses with quantitative monitoring.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding 1.8 nmol/L with raised blocking and modulating antibodies; TSH 0.08 mIU/L with raised free T4 and T3 (still hyperthyroid); TRAb and anti-TPO raised.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, fatigable diplopia, jaw fatigue and nasal voice need AChR antibody testing whatever the thyroid history; current thyroid function matters because hyperthyroidism can aggravate MG and governs the timing of surgery (Jacob 2025; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 11% in deltoid and 14% in nasalis at 3 Hz, normal baseline CMAPs, no post-exercise facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including a facial muscle
action_criteria.rationale: Neurophysiology confirms a postsynaptic transmission defect independently of the thyroid disease and separates MG from thyrotoxic myopathy and LEMS (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Palpebral fissure improves by 3 mm on the right and 2 mm on the left after 2 minutes of ice.
action_criteria.label: Perform an ice pack test on the ptotic lids
action_criteria.rationale: A bedside test that separates fatigable neuromuscular ptosis from the lid signs of thyroid eye disease in a patient with both.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilobed homogeneous anterior mediastinal tissue 3.2 x 1.9 cm without a discrete mass; chemical-shift MRI shows uniform signal loss consistent with thymic hyperplasia.
action_criteria.label: Image the anterior mediastinum for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Every patient with AChR-positive MG needs thymic imaging to detect thymoma, and the finding informs the thymectomy decision (Wolfe 2016). She is overtly hyperthyroid, so iodinated contrast is avoided (ESUR contrast media guidelines): non-contrast CT or MRI is accepted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 3.4 L (98% predicted, 59.6 mL/kg), MIP -64 cmH2O, MEP 88 cmH2O: normal.
action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity and mouth pressures
action_criteria.rationale: She has bulbar fatigue and neck flexor weakness and may receive high-dose steroids, which can transiently worsen MG; a baseline makes later deterioration measurable.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Propranolol adds bradycardia with pyridostigmine and is a beta-blocker caution in MG; methimazole has no NMJ effect; high-dose steroids can transiently worsen MG.
action_criteria.label: Check pyridostigmine against propranolol and methimazole
action_criteria.rationale: She takes a non-selective beta-blocker, which can worsen neuromuscular transmission, and the admitting plan is high-dose IV glucocorticoids; both change management before pyridostigmine or steroids are given.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on coexisting thyroid autoimmunity and MG management.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on MG with autoimmune thyroid disease
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or thyroid eye disease cause before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
Do not give iodinated contrast while she is overtly hyperthyroid.
Do not prescribe a penicillin (documented penicillin allergy).
required_recommendations: Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily and titrate to effect (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily), watching heart rate because she takes propranolol.

Tell ophthalmology and endocrinology that the new ptosis and diplopia are myasthenic; reassess thyroid eye disease activity before IV glucocorticoids, and if IV methylprednisolone is still indicated, give it as an inpatient with daily bulbar and respiratory checks for the first 1 to 2 weeks because high-dose steroids can transiently worsen MG.
Co-manage with endocrinology to reach euthyroidism with methimazole; hyperthyroidism can aggravate MG and must be controlled before surgery.
Review propranolol: keep it only at the lowest dose that controls the tachycardia, monitor for MG worsening, and withdraw it once she is euthyroid.
Refer to thoracic surgery for elective thymectomy (MGTX: AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; CT and MRI show hyperplasia, no thymoma), once MG and thyroid function are stable.
If symptoms persist on pyridostigmine, add prednisone at a low dose titrated upward, with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing) if long-term treatment is needed.

Discuss pregnancy plans before long-term immunosuppression: azathioprine and prednisone are acceptable in pregnancy, mycophenolate and methotrexate are not, and methimazole is replaced by propylthiouracil in the first trimester.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG does not inform a neuromuscular junction disorder.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); nothing suggests Miller Fisher syndrome (no ataxia, normal reflexes) or a CNS process.
FDG-PET has no place in MG; the thymus is characterised by CT and chemical-shift MRI.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class II-III), with comorbid autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves' disease, TRAb-positive) and thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy

differential.diagnosis: Thyroid eye disease as the sole cause of the ptosis and diplopia
differential.key_features: Known thyroid eye disease with proptosis, but ptosis is not a sign of it; here the ptosis is fatigable and improves with ice, diplopia has no restriction on forced duction, RNS shows a decrement and AChR antibodies are positive. The orbitopathy coexists and is part of the diagnosis.
Active hyperthyroidism (TSH 0.08, raised free T4 and T3) may add proximal weakness, but does not cause fatigable ptosis, bulbar fatigue, an RNS decrement or AChR antibodies.
Beta-blockers can worsen neuromuscular transmission but do not cause AChR antibodies; low dose (20 mg twice daily).
Normal baseline CMAPs, no post-exercise facilitation (pathological at 60% or more), preserved reflexes, no autonomic features, AChR antibodies positive.
Proximal limb weakness (shoulders 4/5, hip flexors 4+/5, neck flexors 4-/5), jaw fatigue and nasal voice show generalized disease (MGFA class II-III).
Fatigable, fluctuating signs with a positive ice pack test, limb and bulbar fatigability, and an RNS decrement; no long-tract or sensory signs.

key_clinical_evidence: New fatigable right greater than left ptosis, fatigable non-restrictive diplopia, jaw fatigue, nasal voice and proximal and neck flexor weakness in a woman with Graves disease and thyroid eye disease.
AChR binding 1.8 nmol/L with raised blocking and modulating antibodies, and a 3 Hz decrement in deltoid and nasalis without facilitation: generalized AChR-positive MG coexisting with Graves disease.
She is still hyperthyroid on methimazole (TSH 0.08, raised free T4 and T3), which can aggravate MG and precludes iodinated contrast and elective surgery until controlled.
Planned IV glucocorticoids for thyroid eye disease can transiently worsen MG; the new eye signs are myasthenic, so the indication must be reassessed and any pulse given with monitoring.
Propranolol is a beta-blocker caution in MG and adds bradycardia with pyridostigmine.
Mediastinal imaging shows thymic hyperplasia without thymoma; thymectomy is indicated by MGTX criteria (AChR-positive generalized MG, age 38).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fatigable ptosis with a positive ice pack test, an RNS decrement and AChR antibodies establish coexisting MG; both conditions are present and need separate management.
red_herrings.data_point: Known Graves disease with bilateral proptosis and ophthalmology attribution to thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (CAS 3/7)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all eye signs to thyroid eye disease and proceed to IV glucocorticoids without neuromuscular evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Thyrotoxic myopathy does not cause an RNS decrement or AChR antibodies; both conditions are treated concurrently.
red_herrings.data_point: TSH 0.08 mIU/L, free T4 22.4 pmol/L, free T3 7.8 pmol/L: active hyperthyroidism
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the proximal weakness to thyrotoxic myopathy and defer the MG work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Beta-blockers can worsen MG but do not cause fatigable ptosis with AChR antibodies; the drug is reviewed, not blamed.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the weakness or fatigue to beta-blocker side effects.

findings.description: Non-contrast CT chest; iodinated contrast withheld (requisition: active hyperthyroidism).

Bilobed soft tissue in the thymic bed, 3.2 x 1.9 cm, homogeneous, 38 HU, with preserved arrowhead shape and straight margins. No calcification, no discrete nodular mass, no invasion of adjacent fat or vessels.
Lungs clear. No pulmonary nodule. No pleural effusion.
Mild diffuse enlargement of both thyroid lobes, partly included.

body_imaging.impression: 1. Bilobed homogeneous anterior mediastinal soft tissue, 3.2 x 1.9 cm, without a discrete mass: thymic hyperplasia favoured; thymoma cannot be excluded on CT. 2. Mild diffuse thyroid enlargement. 3. No lymphadenopathy or lung lesion.
recommended_actions: Chemical-shift MRI of the mediastinum recommended to characterise the thymic tissue.

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding, blocking and modulating antibodies elevated; anti-MuSK not detected. TSH suppressed with elevated free T4 and free T3. TRAb and anti-TPO elevated. CBC and metabolic panel within reference range. AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Review of myasthenia gravis: autoimmune thyroid disease is among the most frequent coexisting autoimmune disorders, particularly in early-onset AChR-antibody-positive disease.
results.source: Gilhus NE, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2570-2581

results.finding: International consensus guidance on management: pyridostigmine as initial symptomatic therapy, corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents for persisting symptoms, chest imaging to detect thymoma, and IVIG or plasma exchange for severe or worsening disease.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In the MGTX trial thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522

myasthenia gravis autoimmune thyroid dis.summary: Autoimmune thyroid disease frequently coexists with AChR-positive myasthenia gravis (Gilhus 2016). Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021) recommends AChR antibody testing, electrodiagnostic confirmation and chest imaging for thymoma; MGTX (Wolfe 2016) showed benefit of thymectomy in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes and no post-exercise facilitation. 3. Normal nerve conduction studies. Findings are consistent with a disorder of postsynaptic neuromuscular junction transmission.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: known Graves' disease with thyroid eye disease creates strong anchoring on TAO as sole explanation for all ocular signs; active hyperthyroidism adds thyrotoxic myopathy as a competing explanation for proximal weakness; propranolol on medication list is a third decoy; RNS decrement and AChR positivity disentangle the overlapping diagnoses
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools, 3 red herrings (TAO anchoring, thyrotoxic myopathy, propranolol attribution), requires synthesis across MG serology + thyroid labs + NMJ electrophysiology + medication review to disentangle two coexisting autoimmune processes
metadata.real_seed_note: Demographics and subtype loosely seeded from Patient 2 in PMC5589050 (66-year-old Cantonese female with Graves' + ocular MG + thymoma, PMID 28882932). Case demographics, disease severity, thymic finding, and clinical complexity differ substantially: this case features a 38-year-old East Asian woman with generalized (not purely ocular) MG, no discrete thymoma (thymic hyperplasia only), active hyperthyroidism with thyrotoxic myopathy as additional red herring, and propranolol interaction as a second red herring.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 38-year-old East Asian woman with known Graves' disease (on methimazole) and thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy was admitted after developing new right-sided eyelid droop and double vision over the preceding 6 weeks. She had been diagnosed with Graves' disease 14 months ago after presenting to her primary care physician with palpitations, heat intolerance, and unintentional 5 kg weight loss. Thyroid function confirmed TSH suppression with elevated free T4 and T3; TRAb was markedly positive. She was started on methimazole. Eight months ago, mild proptosis was noted bilaterally (right greater than left) by her ophthalmologist, attributed to thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (clinical activity score 3/7). Selenium was added and artificial tears prescribed. She was told that some degree of eyelid abnormality can occur in thyroid eye disease.

However, over the past 6 weeks she developed a new right eyelid droop she had NOT had before, with a distinctly different character than her proptosis: the lid drooping was worse in the evening and after prolonged activities, and completely resolved each morning after a night of sleep. She also developed intermittent horizontal double vision that she localized to rightward gaze. Both the ptosis and the diplopia were worse after a long day of teaching and resolved after rest. She denied new proptosis, significant orbital pain, or corneal irritation symptoms beyond baseline. She also noticed jaw fatigue when eating tougher foods and her husband noted her voice became nasal after prolonged conversations.

Her endocrinologist and ophthalmologist attributed the new eyelid findings to progressive thyroid eye disease, and she was admitted for IV glucocorticoids. Neurology was consulted because the admitting team found the ptosis to be fatigable on sustained upgaze.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild jaw fatigue reported on prolonged chewing. SpO2 99% on room air. Heart rate 102 bpm, regular.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral proptosis present (right 3 mm, left 2 mm by Hertel exophthalmometry), pre-existing from thyroid eye disease. New bilateral ptosis, right greater than left; levator excursion right 8 mm, left 11 mm. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze: right eye lids descend to mid-pupil at 35 seconds, then complete closure at 55 seconds. Diplopia on rightward gaze. On clinical testing, the diplopia does NOT follow a pattern of restrictive ophthalmoplegia (no mechanical resistance on forced duction testing); instead, it is fatigable — worsens on sustained lateral gaze over 30 seconds. Pupils equal, 4 mm, reactive. No significant conjunctival injection or chemosis today. Mild bilateral facial weakness on grimace. Voice becomes nasal after 3 minutes of sustained speaking.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Normal language and cognition. Mildly anxious.
neurological_exam.motor: Shoulder abductors 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4+/5 bilaterally. Neck flexors 4-/5. Distal strength 5/5. Fatigability documented on sustained arm elevation test. No muscle atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception throughout.

physical_exam.general: Thin, mildly anxious woman. Weight 57 kg, height 163 cm. Warm, moist skin; fine tremor of outstretched hands.
physical_exam.neck: Diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with a soft bruit.
physical_exam.respiratory: Clear to auscultation; no use of accessory muscles.
